claims.text: Prolonged service-relevant thermal or mechanical loading can trigger subtle elemental segregation at grain boundaries in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy.
Grain-boundary segregation can lead to nanoscale intergranular clusters or ordered regions.
The proposed nanoscale intergranular structural changes reduce grain-boundary cohesion.
The proposed nanoscale intergranular structural changes hinder dislocation accommodation.
Reduced grain-boundary cohesion and hindered dislocation accommodation degrade toughness.
The proposed degradation mechanism is distinct from the large-scale precipitate formation typical of conventional alloys.
The initial as-cast alloy is single-phase and has a homogeneous distribution of multiple principal elements.
Controlled thermal aging can promote local chemical clustering without inducing full-scale conventional intermetallic precipitation.
Service-like thermal exposure drives stress-assisted elemental segregation at grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary segregation promotes the nucleation of nanoscale clusters.
Nanoscale grain-boundary clusters localize deformation by reducing grain-boundary cohesion.
Localized deformation causes a premature onset of brittle behavior.
Thermally aged material will have measurably lower fracture toughness than the as-cast baseline.
The predicted toughness decrease will be associated with the appearance of nanoscale grain-boundary clusters.
The as-cast, single-phase baseline has high toughness and a homogeneous microstructure.
Extremely high temperatures or severe deformation may activate degradation mechanisms additional to the proposed segregation-mediated mechanism.

contradictions.description: The exposure is specified as occurring under no or low mechanical strain, while the mechanism characterizes segregation as stress-assisted; the role and source of stress are therefore not consistently defined.
